TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02 that Sam Bankman-Fried cultivated a public image as a young billionaire who "had nothing" eighteen months earlier but then possessed "$22.5 billion" and positioned himself as someone who "was going to spend it to save humanity from extinction." This characterization, described by Michael Lewis in his book "Going Infinite," presented SBF as "the richest person in the world under 30" with an ambitious vision to protect humanity from existential risks - an image that Lewis found astonishing to encounter.


---


# SBF's Rapid Wealth Accumulation and Philanthropic Intentions

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02 that Michael Lewis described Sam Bankman-Fried's meteoric rise in an interview, stating "Eighteen months earlier, he had nothing. Now he had $22.5 billion. He was the richest person in the world under 30 [and] he was going to spend it to save humanity from extinction." Lewis was struck by SBF's transformation from having nothing to possessing $22.5 billion in just eighteen months, positioning him as the wealthiest person under 30 with stated intentions to allocate his fortune toward reducing existential risks to humanity.


---


# Government's fraud allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that the U.S. government alleges Sam Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents given to lenders and investors. Prosecutor Thane Rehn stated that "the defendant lied to the world" and characterized Bankman-Fried as a "man who stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims," distinguishing him from the media portrayal of a good-faith crypto entrepreneur.


---


# Bankman-Fried faces trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of collapsed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is on trial for "seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy." The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was "a fraud from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Former Alameda Research head Caroline Ellison, who pleaded guilty to related criminal charges, testified that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes" involving fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering.


---


# FTX Collapse from Peak Valuation to Bankruptcy

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-06 that FTX grew to become the third-largest crypto exchange with a peak valuation of $32 billion before collapsing into bankruptcy. The publication described how the exchange went from its height of success to filing for bankruptcy, detailing the fraudulent activities and mismanagement that led to its downfall. As former federal prosecutor Josh Naftalis explained, the case represents one of the biggest within the crypto space, involving alleged fraud and money laundering by former CEO Sam Bankman-Fried. "The prosecution painted a picture of an empire 'built on lies'" during the trial proceedings, according to TechCrunch's coverage.


---


# Origin of Michael Lewis's SBF Book Through Character Evaluation Request

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02 that Michael Lewis didn't initially set out to write about Sam Bankman-Fried, but was introduced to him in early 2021 by a Berkeley friend who was considering backing FTX and asked Lewis to "evaluate his character." Lewis was so impressed by SBF's apparent brilliance and rapid ascent from having nothing to $22.5 billion that he decided to write about him, leading to over 100 meetings between them over the following two years. "My jaw was on the floor," Lewis said about SBF's transformation into the richest person in the world under 30.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried Faces Seven Fraud and Money Laundering Counts

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-06 that Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of FTX, faces seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering committed while leading FTX and its sister trading firm Alameda Research. The trial proceedings began with jury selection on October 3, with Bankman-Fried set to testify in his own defense. Former colleagues like Caroline Ellison and Can Sun have already provided testimony detailing alleged misuse of customer funds and improper financial practices within the companies.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Criminal Trial Begins October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial began on Tuesday, 2023-10-03, to determine guilt on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. A former federal prosecutor stated "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point." The trial concerns allegations that Bankman-Fried misused customer funds from FTX, the crypto exchange he founded in 2019 that reached a $32 billion valuation before collapsing in November 2022 following revelations about Alameda Research's balance sheet and a bank run triggered by Binance withdrawing $2.1 billion.


---


# FTX Exchange and Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that during opening statements in Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial, prosecutors characterized FTX as an exchange whose customers were told their money was safe while the defense portrayed it as a legitimate, innovative company. The prosecution alleged Bankman-Fried stole billions from customers through his hedge fund Alameda Research, describing him as a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." In contrast, the defense argued FTX was "a very innovative, successful company" and not a Ponzi scheme, presenting Bankman-Fried as a well-intentioned startup founder who acted in "good faith."


---


# Government's Opening Statement Paints Bankman-Fried as Fraudster

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that prosecutor Thane Rehn described Sam Bankman-Fried's public persona one year prior to the October 2023 trial, stating he "oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, and hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David. He repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure." Rehn characterized this image as deception, asserting that "all of that, all of it, was built on lies."


---


# Adversarial Proximity in SBF Trial: Former MIT Friends Testify Against Bankman-Fried

CNBC reported on 2023-10-06 that Sam Bankman-Fried's former MIT classmates and Bahamas housemates testified against him in court. "Two of Sam Bankman-Fried's former friends from MIT, who also worked at crypto exchange FTX while living with the company's founder in the Bahamas, took the stand in a Manhattan courtroom this week to testify against their former classmate, confidant, and boss." The relationship described reflects adversarial proximity, as Gary Wang and Nishad Singh, who had been Bankman-Fried's close associates, became key prosecution witnesses in the fraud trial concerning FTX's alleged defrauding of customers of billions of dollars.


---


# SEC's fraud allegation against FTX centers on Bankman-Fried's misappropriation

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that the Securities and Exchange Commission alleges FTX was a fraud "from the start," with the distinguishing factor being a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." This civil allegation frames the core of the criminal fraud trial against Sam Bankman-Fried, who faces seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The allegation directly ties the exchange's collapse to Bankman-Fried's personal actions rather than broader market conditions or operational failures.


---


# U.S. Attorney's Characterization of Bankman-Fried Fraud Case

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" at a press conference. This characterization came after FTX's collapse in November 2022, which involved fraudulent misrepresentation of FTT token holdings and massive customer fund misuse. Bankman-Fried faces up to 115 years in prison on charges including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering.


---


# FTX Fraud Verdict and SEC Allegations

The Verge reported on 2023-10-28 that Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, was found guilty on seven counts including wire fraud. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." During his testimony, Bankman-Fried faced repeated judicial scolding for not answering questions directly, while also failing to establish proper risk management systems despite operating a financial exchange.

# Helena World Chronicle sues Google for antitrust violations over AI content use

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for D.C. against Google and Alphabet, alleging anticompetitive conduct violating the Sherman Act and other antitrust laws. The complaint claims Google "siphons off" publishers' content, readers, and ad revenue through technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE), Bard AI chatbot, and Knowledge Graph. Helena World Chronicle argues these practices constitute content misappropriation that harms publishers' bottom lines, with AI potentially reducing publisher website traffic by 20-40% as Google keeps users within its "walled garden" instead of directing them to original sources.


---


# The Verge's 2023-11-01 Report on SEO Practitioners and Internet Search Quality

The Verge reported on 2023-11-01 that SEO practitioners are widely blamed for degrading internet search quality, with Google Search results described as "absolutely unusable" and "garbage." The article profiles the SEO community through interviews and observations, challenging the "hustler" stereotype while exploring how search engine optimization has become "insidious." Writer Nilay Patel attended an SEO conference in Florida expecting to find "mechanical monsters" but instead encountered ordinary people. SEO veteran Missy Ward explained that "Google is very clear about what they want" - high-quality content that keeps users engaged. The piece traces SEO's evolution from technical practice to business model that exploits algorithmic preferences, ultimately questioning whether practitioners or Google itself bear responsibility for search quality decline.


---


# Publisher Alleges Google's AdSense Rate Changes Harm Publishers Economically

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the complaint additionally alleges that Google's changes to AdSense rates have harmed publishers economically, positioning the rate changes as one more instance of anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising line of commerce. The lawsuit filed by Helena World Chronicle claims these rate changes are part of Google's broader anticompetitive behavior that violates U.S. antitrust law, alongside AI technologies like Search Generative Experience and Bard AI that allegedly divert traffic and revenue away from news publishers.

Others point to SEO specialists who exploit algorithms to boost rankings, with one tech writer describing the internet as a "search-optimized hellhole." This internal data shows that homepage market share directly influences search market share, with Google's VP Nitin arguing that focusing on homepage placement was "one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share."

# Default Search Engine as Scarce Distribution Asset

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to device makers like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to become the default search engine on their platforms. A default search engine is "the query service preselected by a device or browser maker so that a user searches through it without taking any setup action, making the placement itself the scarce asset that distributors sell." The U.S. government's antitrust trial argues this practice blocks competition in search and advertising markets. Google defended these payments as necessary to collect data and maintain quality across different devices, with $18 billion alone going to Apple. Internal emails showed Google understood early on that homepage defaults significantly impact search volume, with users doing 15% more searches when defaulting to Google.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google defends its $26.3 billion annual payments to partners like Apple to be the default search engine, arguing this practice is legal because partners choose Google voluntarily. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified that "everybody wants Google as the default engine because it's the best," and that the company pays significant amounts to be ubiquitous so it can collect comprehensive data to maintain its search superiority across different devices. The company's position is that these business arrangements don't constitute illegal monopolistic behavior since consumers benefit from Google's superior search capabilities.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to remain the default search engine across platforms and separately sought to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. These disclosures emerged during the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, revealing how the company uses financial agreements to maintain its search dominance. The report indicates that Google's strategy includes Mobile App Distribution Agreements requiring Android manufacturers to pre-load Google apps including Search and Chrome, though these don't have to be default choices. Additionally, Google has revenue share agreements with smartphone makers and wireless carriers to further secure its market position.

# Google Antitrust Trial Hypothesis on Default Placement vs. Product Quality

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that a central hypothesis in the Google antitrust case is that default search engine placement, rather than product quality, determines market dominance. The government's counterfactual proposition is that "a search engine with comparable product quality and equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale," which would be falsified if a rival given such placement failed to grow market share. This hypothesis challenges Google's defense that its $26.3 billion annual payments to be default search engine across platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla are justified because consumers prefer Google's superior product quality.

The Age reported on 2023-10-22 that when Mozilla made Yahoo the default search engine on Firefox, most users changed it back to Google. This empirical observation was cited by Google in its 2023 trial response as evidence that defaults do not determine user behavior, contradicting claims that Google's dominance stems from default settings rather than user preference.

# Default Search Engine as Scarce Distribution Asset

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to device makers like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to become the default search engine on their platforms. A default search engine is "the query service preselected by a device or browser maker so that a user searches through it without taking any setup action, making the placement itself the scarce asset that distributors sell." The U.S. government's antitrust trial argues this practice blocks competition in search and advertising markets. Google defended these payments as necessary to collect data and maintain quality across different devices, with $18 billion alone going to Apple. Internal emails showed Google understood early on that homepage defaults significantly impact search volume, with users doing 15% more searches when defaulting to Google.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a Arkansas-based publisher filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google, accusing the company of siphoning news content and revenue through anticompetitive practices including AI technologies. Google responded through a spokesperson who rejected the suit as "meritless" and pushed back against the central antitrust and AI-training allegations made by Helena World Chronicle.

# Plaintiffs' Counsel Frames Antitrust Suit Against Google Over AI Harms to Publishers

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that plaintiffs' counsel Hausfeld LLP framed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google as necessary to "restore competition in digital news and reference publishing and to set guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era." The lawsuit invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act for class-wide relief, arguing that Google's AI technologies like Search Generative Experience and Bard are harming publishers' bottom lines by siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue through anticompetitive means.


---


# Google Antitrust Navigation Context: Helena Chronicle Lawsuit and Related Cases

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the Helena World Chronicle's antitrust lawsuit against Google was filed alongside several related legal actions that created a broader regulatory environment. These included the U.S. Department of Justice's existing digital ad technology monopoly suit, the 2020 DOJ civil suit concerning search and search-advertising monopolization, and Epic Games' successful app-store antitrust case. Additionally, Canada had recently reached a news-content settlement with Google requiring payments of "$73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations." TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle accuses Google of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust laws. The suit claims Google "siphons off" publishers' content, readers, and ad revenue through technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot. It alleges that Google's AI integration could reduce publisher website traffic by up to 75%, as users receive answers without clicking through. The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction requiring publisher consent for AI training data usage.

# Google's Multiple Antitrust Cases in Late 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that the complaint additionally alleges that Google's changes to AdSense rates have harmed publishers economically, positioning the rate changes as one more instance of anticompetitive conduct within the digital news advertising line of commerce. The lawsuit filed by Helena World Chronicle claims these rate changes are part of Google's broader anticompetitive behavior that violates U.S. antitrust law, alongside AI technologies like Search Generative Experience and Bard AI that allegedly divert traffic and revenue away from news publishers.


---

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle accuses Google of anticompetitive behavior, specifically arguing that Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) is "designed to keep users inside Google's 'walled garden'" while reusing publishers' content. The complaint contends that SGE was implemented "with the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce."


---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Span Two Markets

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games argues Google restrains competition within two separate markets: "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps." Epic's antitrust lawsuit, beginning November 6, 2023, centers on Google Play's commission structure and restrictive agreements with device manufacturers. Unlike Apple's closed ecosystem, Android allows sideloading, but Epic contends Google makes this process difficult and instead focuses on what it views as anticompetitive practices related to app distribution and in-app payment processing.


---


# Epic v. Google Trial Notes Index - November 6, 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google began November 6, focusing on allegations that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with Google Play. Epic's case relies on the Sherman Act, Cartwright Act, and California's Unfair Competition Law, arguing Google restrains competition in two markets: Android app distribution and in-app payment processing. Key arguments include Google's 15%-30% commission structure, User Choice Billing program, OEM agreements, Anti-Fragmentation Agreements, and developer contracts like "Project Hug." Google counters that it faces competition from other app stores and that its commissions fund security and discovery features.


---


# Epic's Antitrust Trial Against Google Was Four Years in the Making

The Verge reported on 2023-12-12 that Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google "has been four years in the making," originating from a September 2019 email in discovery that outlined a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust issues. The trial lasted four weeks and ended in December 2023 with a jury verdict siding with Epic, finding that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney described the case as his personal fight from the beginning, attending nearly every day of the trial. The plan document from 2019 represented "the causal origin of the proceeding."


---


# Google Bard AI Training Data Allegedly Includes Publisher Content

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed by Helena World Chronicle alleges Google's Bard chatbot was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications." The complaint cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article as sources for this claim, arguing that Google's AI technologies harm publishers' revenues by using their content without consent.


---


# News Publishers Sue Google Over AI Training Data Usage

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit was filed against Google by news publishers, alleging anticompetitive behavior and harm from AI technologies. The complaint cites Google's AI systems like Search Generative Experience and Bard as threats to publishers' revenue, claiming these systems were trained on "news, magazine and digital publications." The lawsuit references a Washington Post analysis conducted with the Allen Institute for AI that found "News and Media sites form the third-largest category of material used in AI training datasets."
